newsitem.title: FIJI: Fiji's new constitution to become law on Friday.
newsitem.headline: Fiji's new constitution to become law on Friday.

text.p: Fiji's new, non-racial constitution will become law on Friday, replacing race-based laws which prevent non-indigenous Fijians from holding high office, President Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara said on Monday.
"With this constitution people of different races, opinions and cultures can live and work together for the good of all...," Mara told the opening of parliament.
Mara said Fiji's leaders had a duty to tell their people that the new constitution would help unite Fiji and enrich the South Pacific nation through ethnic and cultural diversity.
"In informing the people, I urge you all to devote greater attention to our collective interests of learning to live together and of taking on responsibility for each other."

Mara said he will sign the new constitution, already passed by parliament, on Friday -- the seventh anniversary of the introduction of a racially-biased constitution by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka.

Rabuka staged a military coup in 1987, overthrowing the then Indian-dominated government, and subsequently introduced a racially-biased constitution which guaranteed indigenous Fijians control of the parliament.
Under the new constitution, a new 71-seat parliament will see 23 Fijian seats, 19 Indian seats, three for mixed races, one for Rotuma Islanders and 25 open seats for any race.
It will also open the way for a multi-racial government and permit a non-indigenous Fijian to become prime minister.
Rabuka, with the support of Indian-based opposition parties, has said he would seek a multi-racial cabinet under the new constitution, but not until after the next election in 1999.

Indians, who were brought to Fiji at the turn of the century to work on sugar plantations, now make up 45 percent of the country's 750,000-strong population and are influential in the business community.
